issues.legal_issue: A murder charge cannot be discharged at the initial charge stage by deciding the connection between an assault and death solely from a post-mortem report before the prosecution has presented its oral evidence.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that the accused assaulted the deceased during an incident and that she died later that night.
The post-mortem report attributed death to cardio-respiratory failure and recorded no serious injuries.
The trial court discharged the murder charge and framed a lesser homicide charge based principally on the medical material, without hearing the eyewitnesses or the medical officer as witnesses.
The High Court affirmed that decision.
issues.conclusion: The trial court and High Court had effectively conducted a mini trial and reached a premature conclusion about the cause of death. Their orders were set aside, and the trial court was directed to reconsider the charge in accordance with law; the Supreme Court did not decide whether the eventual offence was murder or culpable homicide.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 227 and 228 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the court must judicially sift the prosecution material to decide whether there is ground for presuming that the accused committed the offence; strong suspicion founded on material can suffice, but the court must not conduct a mini trial or determine guilt. The material is generally taken at face value, without a meticulous assessment of its probative value. A post-mortem report is not substantive evidence by itself: the doctor’s testimony is substantive, and the report may be used to corroborate, refresh memory, or contradict that testimony under Sections 157, 159, and 145 of the Evidence Act, 1872. The court relied on Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal, State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh, Dipakbhai Jagdishchandra Patel v. State of Gujarat, Sajjan Kumar v. CBI, Asim Shariff v. National Investigation Agency, State of Karnataka v. M.R. Hiremath, State of Tamil Nadu v. N. Suresh Rajan, Bhawna Bai v. Ghanshyam, Amit Kapoor v. Ramesh Chander, and State of Maharashtra v. Som Nath Thapa.

predicates.sessions_case_charge_stage: The court is deciding whether to frame or discharge a charge before the trial evidence has been heard.
predicates.prosecution_material_alleges_assault_and: The prosecution material alleges an assault on a person and a subsequent death.
predicates.eyewitness_or_expert_evidence_remains_to: Eyewitness or expert testimony relevant to the alleged offence has not yet been presented and assessed at trial.
predicates.higher_charge_discharged_on_postmortem_a: The court discharged the higher charge by relying on the post-mortem report alone to decide the connection between the alleged conduct and death.

issues.definition: When a higher charge in a sessions case is discharged at the initial stage solely on a post-mortem report while relevant eyewitness or expert evidence remains to be heard, the discharge order is set aside.

issues.legal_issue: Framing only a lesser charge restricts the prosecution to presenting evidence on that charge, so the prosecution should be allowed to present its original case where the charge is reconsidered before trial.
material_facts: The prosecution’s original case alleged an assault that resulted in the deceased’s death and the charge sheet sought a murder charge.
The trial court discharged the murder charge and framed a lesser homicide charge before the prosecution had presented its evidence at trial.
The accused would be entitled to confine their defence to the charge framed, while the prosecution would be unable to lead evidence beyond that charge.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was directed to pass a fresh order framing charge in accordance with law. The Court considered it more prudent in the circumstances to permit the prosecution to lead evidence in accordance with its original case, while leaving the ultimate classification of the offence to be decided after the evidence is evaluated.
issues.legal_principle: A charge defines the foundation and scope of the trial: the prosecution may lead evidence only in accordance with the charge, and an accused need answer only the charge framed. If a lesser charge is framed instead of a higher charge supported by the prosecution case, the prosecution may be prevented from presenting evidence beyond the lesser charge. At the charge stage, the court should therefore consider the prosecution’s original case under the standard in Sections 227 and 228 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; the accused may still contend after trial that the proved offence is lesser than the higher charge.

predicates.criminal_trial_charge_stage: The court is deciding the charge before the prosecution has presented its trial evidence.
predicates.prosecution_seeks_to_prove_higher_offenc: The prosecution’s case seeks to establish an offence more serious than the lesser charge under consideration.
predicates.higher_charge_supported_by_prosecution_c: The prosecution material provides a basis for considering the more serious charge.
predicates.only_lesser_charge_would_limit_prosecuti: Framing only the lesser charge would prevent the prosecution from presenting evidence directed to the more serious charge.

issues.definition: When the prosecution seeks to prove a higher offence supported by its case and framing only a lesser charge would restrict its evidence, the prosecution is allowed to present evidence on its original case.
